newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank raps SEC for delayed Bangladesh crisis handling.
newsitem.headline: World Bank raps SEC for delayed Bangladesh crisis handling.

text.p: The World Bank has criticised the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for its slow response to recent upheavals in Bangladesh's capital market, which one one bank official said cost some small investors everything.

In a report on the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) and the SEC, the World Bank said the market began its heady ascent soon after general elections last June that brought Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to power.
Between June and October, the DSE all-share price index jumped from less than 1,000 points to more than 3,600.
It stood at 1,847 points at the close of trade on Thursday.

"Once the market gained the initial momentum, it formed into a bubble," said the World Bank report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters. "Trading (had) moved to the kerb with thousands of retail investors active each day.
It noted that until such a speculative bubble bursts, investors are gripped by the mistaken belief that the market will continue to rise indefinitely.
But the World Bank also pointed its finger at the SEC for being slow in moving to dispell the illusion.

"The SEC was late in reacting. Only in early October did it launch a publicity campaign warning investors of the risks and provide the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) with a list of 24 high-risk companies."
The report noted that investors ignored the warnings and companies targeted accused the SEC of intervention and threatened to sue it for potential losses in their share values."

"Bangladesh scrips (became) some of the most expensive in the world," the report said. "Quasem Dry Cells's return was 1200 percent, Beximco's was 638 percent, Apex Foods' was 550 percent, Beximco Pharma 416 percent and Bangladesh Thai Aluminium 400 percent."
It said that when the SEC imposed "circuit breakers", or caps on share price fluctuations, the market corrected briefly but soon began to test fresh highs.
Only on November 5 did it impose a tougher circuit breaker and the market has since then been bearish, the World Bank said.
"A precipitous fall in the market will expose the small investors with pressures on the government to bail them out,"the World Bank report said.
The report said the DSE was "still a relatively nascent and shallow market" with only 211 listed companies, noting that even at the its peak "only about 120 securities were actively traded".
One World Bank offical, who declined to be named, said that "as a reult of the SEC's delayed response, thousands of small investors have lost everything.
At present the market's capitalisation is around $3 billion, but even at a capitalisation of $6 billion recorded during the peak, it is still lower than that of India and Pakistan, it added.
DSE chairman Imtiyaz Husain declined to comment on the report, but said he expected Bangladesh's capital markets would be gradually bolstered.
"The volume of trading will rise at least four to five times after the DSE computerises in October," he told Reuters.
